sections.heading: Fence Row Clearing for Farms and Rural Properties
sections.body:
Bellhouse Excavating clears old fence rows and overgrown field edges for farm operations and rural property owners across Brant County and Brantford. Old fence lines collect decades of growth — brush, volunteer trees, tangled wire, rotted posts, and stone that a bush hog or a chainsaw crew can't fully deal with. Bellhouse clears the growth, pulls the stumps and roots, cleans up the old wire and posts, and grades the reclaimed strip so it's actually usable — for replacement fencing, wider field access, or simply more workable acreage.

This isn't a mowing or brushing service. Bellhouse brings excavators and a dozer to a fence row job, which means stumps and roots come out instead of getting cut off at grade, buried stone and debris get pulled and hauled, and the ground gets graded once the clearing is done. The result is a fence row that's actually cleared, not one that grows back in two seasons.

cards.title: Old farm fence rows and abandoned fence lines
cards.body: A strong fit when a fence row hasn't been maintained in years and has grown into a solid line of brush, saplings, and volunteer trees along the old fence. Bellhouse clears the growth, pulls the old fence and posts, and reclaims the strip.
cards.outcome: The old fence line is cleared down to usable ground instead of a brushed-back thicket that grows back the same season.

cards.title: Clearing ahead of replacement fencing
cards.body: Useful when a farm is putting in new fence and needs the old line cleared first — brush, stumps, old wire, and rotted posts removed so the new fence contractor has a clean, graded line to work with.
cards.outcome: A cleared, graded fence line ready for new posts and wire, with the old material hauled off or piled as directed.

cards.title: Reclaiming field edges and opening field access
cards.body: A practical fit when brush and volunteer growth along a field edge is eating into usable acreage or blocking equipment access between fields. Clearing and grading pushes the field edge back to where it should be.
cards.outcome: More usable field width and a clear equipment path between fields instead of brush encroaching further every year.

cards.title: Brush, stump, and debris cleanup on rural property
cards.body: A strong fit for hobby farms and rural properties with brush piles, stumps, stone accumulation, or general fence-row debris that's built up over years and needs equipment to actually clear it out.
cards.outcome: The area is cleared, the debris is dealt with, and the ground is left graded and usable instead of just cut back.

sections.heading: Best Fit & Not the Best Fit
sections.subheading: Fence row clearing works best on farm and rural properties where equipment can access the line and the goal is real ground reclamation, not just tree removal.

items.title: Best fit: Old, overgrown farm fence rows
items.body: Fence lines that have grown in with brush, saplings, and small trees over years of no maintenance. Properties in Brant County, Paris, St. George, Burford, Scotland, Oakland, Mount Pleasant, and surrounding rural areas.

items.title: Best fit: Clearing ahead of new or replacement fencing
items.body: Fence rows being cleared before a fencing contractor installs new fence. The line is cleared, old material removed, and the strip graded so the new fence goes in on clean, usable ground.

items.title: Best fit: Field-edge and access-lane clearing
items.body: Brush and growth encroaching on field edges or blocking equipment access between fields, where clearing and grading recovers usable acreage or opens an access route.

items.title: Best fit: Stump, root, and debris removal along a fence line
items.body: Properties where a bush hog or chainsaw crew has already cut the brush back but stumps, roots, old wire, and stone are still in the ground and need equipment to actually pull and clear.

items.title: Not the best fit: Specialty tree work, arborist services, or forestry management
items.body: Bellhouse clears fence rows and field edges with excavation equipment — it does not provide arborist services, selective forestry management, tree health assessments, or environmental consulting. Larger woodlot or forestry projects should go to a licensed forestry contractor.

items.title: Reviewed case by case: Clearing near watercourses, wetlands, or treed hedgerows with environmental significance
items.body: Fence rows that run through or near a watercourse, regulated wetland, or a hedgerow with significant tree cover may fall under conservation authority or municipal tree-removal rules. Bellhouse can review the site, but any required approvals need to be confirmed and in place before clearing begins.

factors.title: Fence-row length
factors.body: Longer fence lines mean more clearing, more stumps, and more material to move. A short field-edge run is a different scope than a quarter-mile overgrown line.

factors.title: Brush, tree, and stump density
factors.body: Light brush clears quickly. Established saplings and volunteer trees with real root systems take more excavator time to pull cleanly.

factors.title: Old wire, posts, and buried debris
factors.body: Fence rows with intact wire, steel or wood posts, and buried stone take more time to clear and separate than a line that's mostly grown-in brush.

factors.title: Material staying on site or hauled away
factors.body: Piling cleared brush and debris on the property costs less than loading and trucking it off site. Bellhouse quotes both ways depending on what you need.

factors.title: Grading after clearing
factors.body: Filling stump holes and rough grading the cleared strip adds machine time but is what actually leaves the ground usable instead of torn up.

sections.heading: What Proper Fence Row Clearing Prevents
sections.subheading: Brushing or mowing a fence row without pulling what's underneath just delays the problem — it doesn't solve it.

items.problem: Brush cut back with a mower or brush hog grows back within a season because the roots were never removed.
items.solution: Bellhouse pulls stumps and root systems with excavators so the growth doesn't come right back the following year.

items.problem: Old fence wire left tangled in cleared brush creates a hazard for equipment and livestock and makes the area unusable.
items.solution: Old wire, posts, and fence material are pulled and cleared as part of the job, not left buried in the debris.

items.problem: A fence row that's been cut back but never graded is still too rough to drive equipment across or run new fence along.
items.solution: Bellhouse fills stump holes and grades the cleared strip so the ground is actually usable when the job is finished.

items.problem: A highway dump truck gets stuck or simply can't reach a soft, wet, or low-lying stretch of a fence row, stalling the job halfway through.
items.solution: Bellhouse brings the off-road haul truck to move cleared material through ground a standard dump truck would get stuck in, so the job keeps moving regardless of field conditions.

sections.heading: Farm fence row clearing by service area
sections.body: Farm fence row and field-edge clearing services are available across Brant County and surrounding rural areas — including Brantford, Paris, St. George, Burford, Scotland, Oakland, Mount Pleasant, Cambridge, and nearby farming communities where old fence lines need real equipment to clear.

items.question: How much does farm fence row clearing cost in Brant County?
items.answer: Fence row clearing cost depends on the length of the line, how heavy the brush and tree growth is, how many stumps and how much old wire and post material need to be pulled, and whether the cleared material stays on site or gets hauled away. A short, lightly grown-in field edge is a different scope than a quarter-mile fence row with established trees, tangled wire, and buried stone. Bellhouse quotes after reviewing the fence row length, growth, and what's underneath. Photos of the fence line and a rough length estimate help Bellhouse return an accurate number.

items.question: Do you just cut the brush back, or actually clear the fence row?
items.answer: Bellhouse clears the fence row — that means pulling stumps and root systems out of the ground, not just cutting brush flush with a mower or brush hog. A bush hog knocks growth down for a season, but the roots stay in the ground and the brush comes back. Because Bellhouse uses excavators, the stumps and roots come out, old wire and posts are pulled, and the ground is graded afterward so the strip is actually usable — not just temporarily cut back.

items.question: What happens to the old wire, posts, and stone after clearing?
items.answer: Old fence wire, wood and steel posts, and any stone or debris pulled from the fence row are separated during clearing and either hauled off site or piled on the property, depending on what you need. Bellhouse can load and truck the material away using highway and tri-axle trucks, or leave it piled in a location that works for the farm operation. This is confirmed during the site review before work begins.

items.question: Can you grade the area after the fence row is cleared?
items.answer: Yes. Grading after clearing is a standard part of the job, not an add-on. Once the brush, stumps, and old fence material are removed, Bellhouse fills stump holes and rough grades the cleared strip using the dozer, so the ground is level and usable — whether that's for new fencing, wider field access, or simply reclaimed acreage. Clearing without grading leaves torn-up ground that's still hard to use.

items.question: Do I need a permit to clear an old fence row?
items.answer: Most farm fence row clearing on private agricultural land doesn't require a permit, but fence rows that run through or near a watercourse, a regulated wetland, or a hedgerow with significant tree cover may fall under conservation authority or municipal tree-removal rules. Property owners are responsible for confirming any required municipal, conservation authority, or other approvals before work begins. Bellhouse can review the site and flag anything that looks like it may need a closer look, but does not provide permitting or environmental consulting services.
